title: Bishop's Opening | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: The pawn to e4, e5 — a pretty high-rated opponent, which is fine with me.
The bishop to c4 — the Bishop's Opening, intimidating to many; it's the opening where White develops the bishop first.
React no differently than against the Vienna: since White didn't play the knight to f3, we don't need to start with the knight to c6 — we play the knight to f6, exploiting that.
d3 — again, many possible schemes of development.
There's a line with c6, which I won't play; the simplest is just to develop the other knight with the knight to c6.
After the knight to f3 we've transposed into an Italian; with the bishop to c5 it's a full Italian, or we can play the bishop to e7, slightly more passive.
I'll play the bishop to e7 — perfectly viable, and we're playing very solid; some practice in these dry positions.
The knight to c3. We can play d6 or castle — the order really doesn't matter.
Let's go d6 and then castle.
h3, and we castle — the Hungarian Variation: quite passive but extremely solid, no weaknesses, relatively symmetrical.
White's bishops are marginally better placed, but we'll try to neutralize that. We have one undeveloped piece left — would the bishop to e6 be justified? Is that trade something to fear?

In Italian positions, opening the f-file is generally good for the side that controls it, even at the cost of doubled pawns. So the bishop to e6 is rarely a move to refrain from over the bishop takes c6 — never dangerous; after the recapture our doubled e-pawns control important squares, and we get free f-file pressure. The other advantage: if White continues the standoff, we don't have to take on c4 —
— we can actually break through in the centre with d5, gaining space. A tough situation for White — and he takes.
We take, and I already like Black's position here.

One comment: White isn't castled yet — we need to be prepared for castling in either direction. Many good approaches: the queen to e8, aiming for g6 if he castles short; or more ambitiously a6 to prepare a pawn storm if he castles queenside; and if he castles kingside, a6 is still a helpful move.

d5 is probably what I'd play over the board, but for solid style, a6 — flexible, it doesn't hurt to control b5, and if he castles queenside we jump-start our pawn storm with b5. If he castles short, we'll have clear ways to pressure down the file.

a5 would weaken b5. g4 is a blunder — it drops a pawn. Instructive: two ways to win it immediately. The knight on f3 is left undefended — this screams discovery tactic; there are two: the knight takes g4, or the knight takes e4.

After the knight takes g4 and the pawn recaptures, we open the h-file for him — not advisable, since he'll probably castle queenside. Much better to take the centre pawn: we open no avenues on his kingside. He takes, we take the knight on f3.

It's a good idea to make sure your rook doesn't get trapped on f3 — but with the whole f-file, we have nothing to fear, and we're up a pawn. After any pawn trade, ask how the position changed: with the e-pawn gone, the move d5 becomes much stronger.

d5 looks extremely appealing — it sends the knight back, and then d4 might trap the bishop on e3; d5 is our default reaction. The bishop to g5 — d5 still looks great: he'll take the bishop, we recapture with the queen —
— chasing the knight out of the centre. I see no reason to refrain; takes, takes, then we bring the other rook to f8.
Already very depressing for White — the knight to d4 was also great. He takes.
We take, obviously with the queen. This'll go the knight to g5, further exacerbating the situation.
I'd love to reroute the knight to f4, but it's very hard, since e6 is blocked by a pawn. Where does the rook go? A lot of people default to the rook to f8, but don't rush to bring the rook back —

— notice the queen defends the knight; our queen pressures it, and the rook to f4 slices off the connection — the knight is simply trapped. He's got to go h4, giving up another pawn, and White's position collapses.

If he goes h4, another interesting moment. The obvious rook takes g4 opens the g-file — he'd likely castle and seek counterplay, though the g-file alone is unlikely to be enough for two pawns — but an idea is h6 first, kicking the knight, then take on g4, dulling his kingside initiative.
We also have a third approach — we don't have to touch any of that; play the knight to d4, or more incisive, the rook from a8 to f8. The knight to f4 isn't going anywhere.
The knight to d4 doesn't threaten anything, which bothers me a little, because this square is protected by White's knight, and he can play c3.
Don't rush to bring our pieces to central squares; the rook to f8 creates a big threat of the rook takes f2, forcing him to commit further, then we decide.
All these moves are good — h6, the rook takes g4, the knight to f4; don't bog yourself down figuring out which is better —

— often it's two or three valid alternatives, a matter of taste. Why is the rook to f8 a threat? It's not just two rooks for the queen — after the trades we win a bunch of pawns on top, and there's a fork: the queen to c5 with check —
— then we take c2, a common queen fork at the end of a line, like a famous game. c4 does a whole lot of bad — first, it permanently weakens the d4-square —

— so I love the idea of slamming the knight into d4. We can still play the rook takes f2, nothing wrong with that, but now we can squeeze a lot more by bringing our pieces to dominant squares; pawns don't go backwards, so he can never chase us from d4. We threaten h6 followed by the knight to f3 with a fork. The queen takes g5 is a decent winning endgame, but play to win economically — h6 chases the knight; don't be fancy just to force liquidation, find the most efficient win.
If he castles, we take f2 with a devastating second-rank attack. I like that we still have a pawn on a6 from a past life. The rook to h3 doesn't substantively change anything —
— we can still go h6; in fact the knight is now simply trapped, which is kind of funny. This might be resigns.
The knight takes e6.
We keep the knight on d4 and take with the queen. Resigning is a very good option here.
He takes on d5. We can take g4 or take d5 — it absolutely doesn't matter, as long as we're taking something.
Let's take g4 — that seems more incisive, hitting the rook, and if the rook to g3, we have a nice tactic to finish the game.
The rook to g3. What's important is that the knight is taking a square away from the king —
— that's the second ingredient, with our doubled rooks and queen: the queen takes g3 ends the game, the rook to f1 being checkmate.
He castles — let's just take on f2.
The queen takes f2 — we could have taken the rook, but —
— this simplifies the position.

How did I see that so quickly? That's where puzzles come in — with endless puzzle-solving at the beginning of your development, you'll find these moves even without knowing how you found them; that's how pattern recognition works.

A relatively easy game. One thing I wanted to explain: why d5 is so powerful — often you'll see people play the bishop to b3, and then d5 is very strong, particularly because his two minors are placed awkwardly and d4 becomes a fork threat; after a trade on d5, Black just has a great position. On a6 versus a5: a6 is more flexible, keeping the option of attacking the queenside, whereas a5 locks things up too soon. And I chose the bishop trade because I was a little concerned my e5-pawn might become weak.
